name: The Murray household — a name from the post office's letter lists
head: murray_alonzo

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RETURN, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The office's list of letters uncalled-for is a RETURN — its statement of what was still unclaimed on ONE day — and the paper reprinted one return over as many consecutive issues as it took, so the bound is dated by the return of 1 July 1834 and not by the issue it was read in (T-0425). The earliest issue this project reads the name in is 1834-07-02, 1 day later; that gap is an accident of which impression an extraction pass reached, and it is not evidence. Somebody was writing to this name at Chicago by 1834-07-01 and at no stated time before it; nothing says when they came. The date lines the printings set, and how they were weighed, stand beside this rule in tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py.

lives_at.note: Not attested: a letter list gives a name and no address.

works_at.note: Not attested. No trade is recorded, so there is no premises to seek.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Nothing after 1834-07-16 follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. `uncertain` rather than dropped — the distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and a finding, not a gap.

persons.name: Alonzo Murray

occupation.note: No source records an occupation for this person. A list of uncalled-for letters prints a name and no trade, and this pass will not read one in.

persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G1b, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is attested because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). FIRST READ AT THE POST OFFICE, AND THE CORPUS NAMES THEM AGAIN (T-1005). The papers print 'Alonzo Murray' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 29, reprinted over 3 consecutive issues — dated 1834-07-02 to 1834-07-16. THE CORPUS NAMES THIS PERSON BESIDE THE RETURN: 1 ordinary reading of the papers, not a list of uncalled-for letters — the Democrat of 24 September 1834 (‘Murray, A.’, chicago_democrat_1834_09_24#c005). That is why `letter_list_only` is no longer written on this record: the flag says ‘known only from the post office’ and this record says otherwise. The return below still stands, and is still the weakest thing said here. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

conflicts: Committed refusals stand against every other Murray reached — St Mary's 'John Murray', the 1834 poll's 'Patrick Murray', Fergus 1839.

merge_ruling.for_merge: Murray and Murry differ by one letter and both cards read “Alonzo”, which is an uncommon forename — the town holds one other Alonzo in the whole resident layer. Two uncommon forenames on one stem inside a year is the shape a duplicate usually takes.
merge_ruling.against_merge: THREE THINGS, AND THE FIRST TWO WOULD BE ENOUGH. (1) TWO RETURNS, AND THE EARLIER IS SET THREE TIMES. “Alonzo Murray” stands on the return of 1 July 1834 and is printed in the impressions of 2, 9 and 16 July 1834, all three reading “Alonzo Murray”; “Murry, Alanzo 2” stands on the return of 31 March 1835, printed 20 May 1835. No return sets both. (2) THE FORENAMES ARE NOT IDENTICAL AS PRINTED. The 1835 line reads ALANZO, not Alonzo; the cards agree only after this project's own normalizer folded the o/a. So the pair that town_pairs joined on an identical forename does not have one on the page, and a merge would be folding two letters, not one. (3) MURRAY IS A POPULATED SURNAME AT THIS TOWN WHERE MURRY IS NOT. The corpus carries Nelson Murray (return of 1 April 1834), “A, MURRAY” in the Democrat of 24 September 1834 and James H. Murray in the American of 20 June 1835, and the resident layer carries a Patrick Murray card besides; the only Murry of any forename is this one. A surname several families bear is not a slip for a surname one man bears, and the direction of the supposed error is therefore unargued. D6, and the cards stay two.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.
